corrections.workload: thread-ring (Computer Language Benchmarks Game spec): 503 ring members pass a token 5,000,000 times (input in benchmarks/run_all.py); essentially single-threaded and bound by context-switch cost. Paper table reported for a 32-core machine (snippet).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Thread-ring on 32 cores (snippet only, paper Table 5): Erlang 3.30 s versus the paper's C++/TBB column 34.13 s, about 10.3x (derived from the snippet numbers); the C++ program is Boost.Asio over 503 OS threads.
corrections.caveats: Paper numbers seen only through WebSearch result summaries (Table 5 of arXiv 1405.7153, 'Efficient and Reasonable Object-Oriented Concurrency', West, Nanz and Meyer, published at ESEC/FSE 2015): thread-ring on 32 cores Erlang 3.30 s, SCOOP/Qs 5.82 s, Go 13.98 s, C++/TBB 34.13 s, Haskell 57.44 s; arxiv.org is blocked here, so the table, CPU model and compiler versions were not opened. The benchmark code is public in https://github.com/scottgw/quicksilver/tree/master/benchmarks/concurrent (cxx, go, erlang, haskell, qs, java), and all thread-ring programs are Computer Language Benchmarks Game submissions. The C++ side is not TBB: it is the Benchmarks Game Boost.Asio program with 503 OS pthreads waiting on one shared io_service queue, so every token pass is an OS-level futex wake-up and context switch, while Erlang passes the token between BEAM processes inside a user-space scheduler. The win is green threads against OS threads (runtime, not codegen); a C++ ring on Boost.Fiber, Boost.Context or a single-threaded loop was not measured and would very likely beat both. The C++ build is -O3, so the baseline is not crippled by flags, but the comparison is of threading models. Timing asymmetry in benchmarks/run_all.py: Erlang's TotalTime is its own timer:tc figure printed to stderr (excludes VM boot and shutdown), while C++, Go and Haskell are wall-clock around Popen including process launch and, for C++, creating 503 pthreads; small against multi-second runs but it favours Erlang. The repo's run_all.py at HEAD runs the concurrent tasks with worker_range = [4], while the snippet says the paper table is for 32 cores, so the exact configuration of the published run is not certain. Toolchains date from about 2014 (BEAM without JIT). Lead for a paper-access retier.
corrections.why_faster: From the sources: the Erlang program (Benchmarks Game, Jiri Isa) passes the token by message send between 503 BEAM processes, scheduled in user space without kernel involvement, while the C++ program parks 503 OS pthreads on one boost::asio::io_service queue so each pass is a mutex/condition-variable hand-off with a kernel futex wake and OS context switch, often across cores. Runtime threading model, not compiler codegen.
